1:
None of the prophecies from here on are dated, as Gill and Henry note, and both place this one after the destruction of the city, when it would be seasonable to ask what had caused it. Keil and Delitzsch head it as the opening of the promise of salvation for the covenant nation after the judgment: the Lord will deliver Israel from its evil shepherds, who feed only themselves and destroy the flock, will gather and tend his own on a good meadow, protect the weak against the strong, and through his servant bring security to the whole flock; and they trace the promise developing through the chapters that follow.

Who the shepherds are is agreed but variously filled in. Gill takes them for the political governors, kings and princes and magistrates of every degree, and also the ecclesiastical, prophets and priests and scribes, noting that among the eastern nations and the Greeks alike it was common to call kings shepherds, one Greek word serving both for feeding sheep and for governing people. Clarke divides them the same way and makes the flock the whole people. Wesley limits the people meant to the two tribes and the few of the ten who adhered to the house of David. Henry insists they are but under-shepherds, accountable to the great Shepherd of Israel, and that dignity and power which do not keep men from sin will not exempt them from reproof.

The first charge is self-service. Clarke reads the fat and the wool as the tithes and offerings on one side and the taxes and imposts on the other, both diverted: the priests using the offerings not to further their ministry but to pamper themselves, the state using the revenue not for justice and government but to subsidise foreign powers and maintain its own luxury. Gill and Clarke both report that the word for fat differs from the word for milk only in the pointing and that several ancient versions read milk, which Clarke thinks right.

The second charge is neglect, and Clarke turns it into an examination of the office. No one is fit to be a shepherd who does not know the diseases sheep are liable to and how to cure them; and no one is fit for the pastoral office who does not know the disease of sin, the remedy, and how to administer it, since he who does not know the Saviour cannot recommend him, and he who is not saved will not save. A proper shepherd, he says, can set a broken bone and bind it till it knits, as a pastor knows how to restore one overtaken in a fault, such sudden falls being to the soul what a broken bone is to the body; and he knows his sheep individually and counts them often, so that a stray cannot get far before he goes after it. Gill reads the same clauses twice over, once of the poor and captive left unrelieved in the state, and once of the weak in faith left unstrengthened by their teachers.

On the scattering Ellicott is careful about blame: the calamities are laid at the door of the rulers, not because the people were sinless, which the book has abundantly denied, but because their sins were largely due to the example, the idolatries and the oppressions of those over them. Gill says there were shepherds, but idol shepherds, good for nothing, so that it was all one as if there were none. Clarke says discipline failed, the flock became disorganised and separated in affection and fellowship, and grievous wolves seized on them. Ellicott distinguishes the two verbs, to ask after and to search out, and concludes that the first act of mercy to such a flock must be the removal of the unfaithful shepherds.
7:
The shepherds are summoned twice, and Gill takes the repetition as confirmation, that what follows may be depended on unless they change their conduct, and as leaving them inexcusable. Henry reads the passage as a display of two feelings at once, indignation at the shepherds and tenderness toward the flock, and says the summons itself is humbling: those who will not hear the word of the Lord giving them their direction shall be made to hear it reading them their doom, and shall learn how little he regards them who made much of themselves, and how much he regards the flock they made nothing of. Clarke declines to itemise the bad shepherd at all, since the character can be had by reversing the marks of the good one he has just given.

The sentence is put under oath. Gill says it was sworn in wrath, and reads the declaration bodily, that his heart and his hand and his face were against them. Henry takes up what they had relied on: they had a commission from God to feed the flock and used his name in what they did, expecting him to stand by them; instead he stands against them, since having the name and authority of shepherds will not engage him for those who do not do the work enjoined them. He also traces how the flock was lost twice over, first to the deceivers who drew them into idolatry and then to the destroyers who carried them into captivity, while the shepherds took no care to prevent either, so that it was as if there had been no shepherds at all.

Two penalties follow. The first is an accounting: the flock will be required at their hands and it will be charged upon them that so many are missing, which Henry turns on those who take the care of souls and then take no care of them, ministers being bound to watch and work as men who must give account. The second is deprivation of both the work and the wages, since it is just that the power men have abused and the trust they have betrayed should be taken out of their hands. Henry adds that this alone they could bear well enough, and so it is added that they shall no longer feed themselves either, the flock being delivered out of the mouth of those who instead of protecting it had made a prey of it; those who enrich themselves with the spoils of the public cannot expect to be always allowed to do so. Clarke reads the same sentence historically, that a whole hierarchy which ruled the flock with force and cruelty was once unpriested in his own country and a better qualified set raised up in their place, and warns those who succeeded to be faithful lest the same be done to them.
11:
Ellicott makes this verse carry everything: the rich promises that follow are all contained in the one assurance that the Lord himself will be the shepherd of his flock, which he says must be understood spiritually. Many of the promises are earthly and temporary in form, and he assigns them a layered fulfilment, partly in the return from exile and partly in the deliverance of the church from its foes in the age of the Maccabees; but these were themselves types of a greater deliverance to come, and the means by which it was secured. The promise could only be brought within the comprehension of that people by being set out in earthly language, as we ourselves still need sensible images for glories we cannot otherwise conceive.

The cloudy and dark day is read as a time of general distress by Clarke and Wesley alike, Clarke adding that such times require the shepherd to be especially watchful. Gill describes the shepherd going among a flock gathered again after scattering, to see which are missing and in what condition the rest are. Ellicott insists the phrase is figurative like the rest, so that the gathering to their own land must be explained the same way: the people had wandered in the gloom and are to be gathered back.

Gill gives the restoration a fulfilment in stages. It was in part accomplished when the captivity ended, which he ascribes to God as the one who stirred up the king of Persia to proclaim their liberty and raised the spirit of the people to go up and build; but the fuller accomplishment he places in a later day when they shall be gathered from all countries and saved, and he finds a pledge of it in the crowd from every nation at the feast, and in the practice of preaching first to the Jews wherever the Gospel went among the Gentiles. Clarke expects a holy and diligent priesthood raised up to give sound instruction everywhere, and says plainly that some of these promises belong to the Christian church.

The good pasture Gill takes for the fulness of grace, food suitable to the spirit of a man and enduring to everlasting life, with a variety in it, milk for babes and meat for strong men; and the repetition of the promise he reads as confirmation, the reason being that they are his own flock by right and property. On the seeking of the lost he distinguishes senses: they are lost not to the knowledge and care of God but to their own knowledge of him, unable to help themselves and unaware of their condition until they are enlightened. Against this stands the sentence on the fat and the strong, which Clarke applies to the cruel and imperious shepherds who tyrannised the flock and Wesley to the powerful and rich. Ellicott notes that fatness, generally an emblem of prosperity, stands here for the prosperity that begets hardness of heart, and that feeding with judgment means not with wisdom but with righteousness and authority.
17:
The address turns from the shepherds to the flock, and the first thing done is to divide it. Gill observes that in the church of Israel, as in the visible churches now, there were two sorts, some sheep and some goats. Clarke draws the line between false and true professors, between those who have the form of godliness and those who have its power. Ellicott makes a correction that changes the shape of the passage: the judgment is not between the cattle on one side and the rams and he-goats on the other, but within each class, between one and another of the flock and between one ram and another, so that all the evil of whatever rank are rejected. Wesley reads it as judgment between weaker and stronger as their different states require, and takes the rams for rulers, dealt with according to their behaviour. Henry identifies them as those who, without the power of rulers, were rich enough to bear hard upon their poor neighbours.

The charge is waste as much as greed. Henry states it plainly: the rams and he-goats kept the good pasture to themselves, ate the fat and drank the sweet, and would not let the poor of the flock enjoy the little left, treading down the residue of the pasture and fouling the residue of the water, so that the flock had to eat what had been trodden into the dirt and drink what had been muddied. And this seemed a small thing to them, as if it were the privilege of their quality to injure their neighbours; many who live at ease, he says, care nothing for the straits of those about them, and grudge that anybody should live near them in comfort. Ellicott puts the same in a sentence, that they not only supplied themselves first but with careless insolence destroyed what should have been left for others. Wesley says what they could not eat they wasted, though the deep waters were enough for all. Clarke turns it on those who arrogate all the promises of God and will hardly let a simple believer claim any token of favour, and adds that some would rather feed their sporting dogs than the poor who would be glad of the crumbs.

Worse follows. Henry notes that they thrust with side and shoulder at the feeble, since the weakest goes to the wall, and pushed the diseased with their horns, knowing they could master those they dared not meddle with as equals. He sets an observation of sheep against it, that if one of a flock is sick the rest will shelter it from the heat of the sun, whereas these were most injurious to the diseased; those they could not use they drove out of the country, as if the poor were a public nuisance. It is a barbarous thing, he says, to add affliction to the afflicted.

The judgment is stated in the plainest terms. Clarke reads it as between the rich and the poor, between those who fare sumptuously every day and those who lack the necessaries of life; Wesley says simply that the poor will be vindicated. Gill notes that the flock ate what had been trodden because they could come at nothing else, being as sheep without a shepherd or worse. Henry hears in the promise of salvation a deliverance from both kinds of oppressor, and takes the occasion as the usual one on which the prophets pass to the promise of the kingdom to come; he also suspects the rams and he-goats stand for a later party of teachers who devoured the houses of widows and took away the key of knowledge, since it is no new thing for the flock of God to suffer from those who are themselves of the flock and in eminent stations in it.
23:
Ellicott builds the strongest argument in the chapter on the one shepherd. He is one both against the many evil rulers who went before, which implies the perpetuity of his rule, and against the two kingdoms, which are hereafter to be united; and the prophecy can plainly find no accomplishment in a merely human ruler. On the name he presses a consistency test: if one part of the passage is to be taken literally the rest must be too, so that whoever foretells here a literal restoration of the two kingdoms and their union under one governor must make that governor David himself. The absurdity of that supposition is for him an important piece of evidence that the whole is a promise of spiritual blessing and of the gathering of a people into one flock. He adds that David, as head of the old order and ancestor after the flesh, constantly appears as the type, so that the prophecy must have been so understood even when it was given. Gill and Wesley read the shepherd the same way, Gill calling him the principal one beside whom under-shepherds are not to be named, and one shepherd with respect to Jew and Gentile alike.

Gill takes the promise that the Lord will be their God for the great blessing of the covenant, than which there can be no greater. Clarke draws from the same verse that the call and qualifications of all genuine pastors belong to the prince set over the flock and must be derived from him, so that every minister may seek his credentials there.

On the covenant of peace Clarke gives the philology. The verb is to cut, and he explains the ancient rite behind it: the victim was divided from end to end, the halves laid opposite each other, and the contracting parties entered the space from either end, met in the middle and there took the oath. He reads the evil beasts made to cease as the false and ravenous pastors purged out. Gill takes the covenant as one made from everlasting and now made known to the flock, and Wesley as a covenant of promises which contain and shall bring all good.

Ellicott identifies the hill as Zion and takes the figure at its usual value, that the centre of the old order is always in scripture the centre from which the new covenant goes out; and he supports the continuity with a historical claim, that as many of the Jews embraced the new faith as ever returned from the exile. Clarke reads the shower as the influence of the Spirit and the showers of blessing as light and life and joy and peace in the assemblies. On the plant of renown, which the phrase makes literally a plantation to the name, Clarke allows that it might be applied to a community of believers but thinks it more probably one person, elsewhere called a branch and a rod; Wesley says only that the plant is the Messiah and the shame the reproach. Gill rejects the reading of one authority who made the plant the Jewish nation itself.

The last verse gives the key. Gill says the point of it is that everything in the chapter about sheep and a flock is to be understood not literally but of rational and spiritual persons, chosen and separated and fed in pastures of the Lord own providing; he notes that the rabbis used the same text to argue that only Israelites are called men. Clarke states the equivalences in a line: under the figure of a flock, men; under that of a pasture, the church; under that of a shepherd, the Messiah; and he insists that the God so revealed is the self-existent Being, governor and saviour and judge alike.
